Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1.
$$

Taking $\theta =x$ and substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{cos}^{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int {(2{cos}^{2}⁡x)}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({cos}^{2}⁡2x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the same formula $2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1$ with $\theta =2x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡2x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\frac{3}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+2(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+\frac{3}{2}\,x+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+\frac{3x}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$
